topic: Edward Deci (1971): Soma Puzzle Cubes, Overjustification & How Cash Rewards Undermine Intrinsic Motivation
visual_mode_reason: Deci's one-way mirror free-choice observation (students abandoning Soma puzzle cubes once cash vouchers stop) pairs cleanly with Murayama et al.'s modern fMRI proof of corticostriatal intrinsic-value suppression.

primary_case.title: Edward L. Deci's University of Rochester Soma puzzle free-choice intrinsic motivation experiment
primary_case.place: University of Rochester Department of Psychology, Rochester, New York

people.name: Edward L. Deci
people.role: Psychologist who challenged operant dogma by showing tangible piece-rate pay erodes spontaneous curiosity once withdrawn

people.name: Richard M. Ryan
people.role: Co-founder with Deci of Self-Determination Theory (autonomy, competence, relatedness)

people.name: Kou Murayama
people.role: Neuroscientist whose 2010 fMRI replication showed performance pay physically dampens subsequent striatum-prefrontal intrinsic activity

core_facts.fact: In 1971 at the University of Rochester, Edward Deci invited 24 college students across three one-hour sessions to assemble three-dimensional 'Soma' block puzzles (invented by Piet Hein) into sketched shapes.

In Session 1, nobody was paid; halfway through each session, Deci excused himself for 8 minutes leaving current magazines (New Yorker, Playboy, Time) right beside the Soma blocks while secretly timing through a one-way mirror how many seconds students played with the puzzles FOR FUN.
In Session 2, the experimental group received $1 for every Soma puzzle solved within 13 minutes, while the control group continued solving the exact same puzzles with zero pay.
During paid Session 2, paid students played slightly more during the free break (313.9 seconds vs 205.7 seconds baseline) to practice winning.

The shocker hit in Session 3 when Deci announced study funds had run out so nobody would be paid today: unpaid controls actually INCREASED spontaneous puzzle play slightly (241.2 seconds vs 212.1 in Session 1), whereas formerly paid students DROPPED nearly 50 seconds below their own Session 1 baseline (198.5 seconds vs 248.2 seconds).

In a parallel third experiment inside the exact same 1971 paper, giving students sincere VERBAL PRAISE ('That's very good, much faster than most people') instead of cash INCREASED subsequent unpaid free-choice play.

Across 128 studies later meta-analyzed by Deci, Koestner & Ryan (1999), expected tangible 'if-then' rewards reliably undercut intrinsic interest on enjoyable tasks ('overjustification'), because perceived locus of causality shifts from internal autonomy ('I love puzzles') to external control ('I work for vouchers').

In 2010, Kou Murayama's team scanned this exact 3-stage design in fMRI: removing performance pay caused corticostriatal activation (anterior striatum and lateral prefrontal cortex) during free-choice play to plunge below unpaid controls.

During Session 3's 8-minute (480-second) unobserved free-choice window after Session-2 piece-rate pay ended, unpaid control students spent 241 seconds solving Soma cube puzzles whereas formerly paid students dropped to 198 seconds.

wow_facts.fact: Pay college students for one single hour to solve a 3D puzzle they already loved for free — then stop paying them — and they abandon the puzzle faster than people who never got a dime.
wow_facts.why_surprising: External pay rewrote 'play' into 'unpaid labor' in sixty minutes.

wow_facts.fact: In the exact same 1971 paper, sincere verbal feedback ('you solved that faster than average') boosted unpaid curiosity instead of killing it.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Information that feeds competence uplifts drive; 'if-then' bribes feel controlling.

wow_facts.fact: Decades later inside an MRI scanner (Murayama 2010), the formerly paid group's reward striatum literally went quieter than unpaid controls when playing alone in the waiting room.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Overjustification isn't just an excuse — it dampens intrinsic striatal valuation.

wow_facts.fact: Unexpected surprise bonuses given AFTER a creative project finishes do NOT harm intrinsic motivation at all.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Only dangling an expected 'do X to get Y' carrot shifts autonomy outward.

misconceptions.myth: Adding piece-rate cash bonuses on top of an enjoyable activity always adds extra total motivation ('intrinsic + extrinsic = more').
misconceptions.truth: Intrinsic and controlling extrinsic motivation are NOT strictly additive; expected piece-rate rewards crowd out internal drive once stopped.

misconceptions.myth: All external rewards and salaries destroy human motivation.
misconceptions.truth: Fair base salaries, unexpected 'thank-you' bonuses, and competence-affirming verbal praise preserve or enhance intrinsic interest; dull routine tasks also don't suffer.

misconceptions.myth: Preschoolers are too young to show overjustification.
misconceptions.truth: Lepper, Greene & Nisbett (1973) replicated the exact drop in nursery schoolers promised a 'Good Player Award' ribbon for drawing with felt-tip markers.

misconceptions.myth: People only stop playing in Session 3 out of spite.
misconceptions.truth: fMRI shows silent corticostriatal valuation drops automatically even when subjects aren't consciously resentful.

everyday_hooks: Paying a child per page to read books they already enjoyed — and watching them stop reading the day the summer chart ends.
Turning a beloved photography or baking hobby into a frantic gig-economy side hustle and suddenly dreading picking up the camera.
Using fair base pay + surprise 'here's what you built brilliantly' recognition instead of micromanaged per-ticket bounties.
Keeping one creative project completely unmonetized and untracked just for pure play.
